facts.text: Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn would live if the death rates at each age stayed the same as in the year the baby was born.
In 1900, the average life expectancy at birth for the whole world was about 32 years.
By 2023, world life expectancy had more than doubled, to about 73 years.
Life expectancy more than doubled in every world region over this period.
Before modern times, about one in four babies died before their first birthday, and almost half of all children died before the end of childhood.
The very high number of child deaths in the past was a big reason why average life expectancy was so low; the fall in child deaths has been an important driver of the rise.
A low average life expectancy in the past did not mean that most adults died young: in England and Wales in 1841, a child who had reached age five could expect to live to about 55.
The rise was not only due to fewer child deaths; people began living longer at all ages.
Causes of the rise include better food, clean water, sanitation such as sewers, care for newborn babies, vaccines, antibiotics, economic growth, and less poverty.
Penicillin was discovered in 1928 and became widely available in the 1940s.
In the United States, adding chlorine to drinking water to make it safe began in the early 1900s.
In the United States, children under five made up 30.4 percent of all deaths in 1900 but only 1.4 percent in 1997.
The rise was not smooth: events such as wars, the 1918 flu pandemic, and the COVID-19 pandemic caused clear drops in life expectancy.

In the chart data, Japan's life expectancy at birth was lower than the United Kingdom's in 1900 (38.6 vs 45.6 years) but higher in 2000 and 2023; in 2023 Japan's figure (84.7) was the highest of the four lines.
